introduction-the-second-law-of-thermodyn.core: Left alone, software becomes more disordered: dependencies age, quick fixes accumulate and knowledge leaks away. Order requires continuous energy; disorder is free.

first_principles.problem: Teams assume code that works today stays healthy, then find years later a tangled, outdated system nobody dares touch.
derivation: Make decay **visible** with metrics and automation.

analogy.title: A sandcastle on the beach
analogy.story: Without constant rebuilding, wind and waves flatten it. Nobody has to attack it.
analogy.breaks: Sandcastles can't be protected. Software can, with automation and habits.

example.title: A 5-year-old service
example.scenario: Nobody has touched it in two years.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Small regular upkeep would have cost far less.

example.outcome: you plan for decay instead of being surprised.

check.q: Why does software decay without code changes?
check.a: The world around it changes: dependencies, platforms, security requirements and knowledge.

software-rot-in-practice-how-systems-act.core: Software rots in four ways: dependency rot (the environment drifts), design rot (architecture erodes under quick fixes), knowledge rot (understanding leaves with people) and data rot (formats and assumptions go stale).

first_principles.problem: 'Tech debt' is used as one vague term; without naming the type of rot, teams apply the wrong fix.
truths: Each rot type has a different cause.
derivation: **Data rot** → schema evolution, data quality checks.

analogy.title: A house aging in four ways
analogy.story: Appliances become obsolete, extensions get bolted on awkwardly, nobody remembers where pipes run, and old wiring standards no longer apply.
analogy.breaks: Houses age slowly. Software environments can change in weeks.

example.title: Python 2.7 end-of-life
example.scenario: A service still on Python 2 in 2026.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Scheduled dependency upgrades every sprint would have avoided the cliff.

example.outcome: each type of rot gets its own countermeasure.

check.a: Loss of understanding about a system as people leave and documentation goes stale.

the-broken-window-theory.core: Visible disorder invites more disorder: one ignored lint warning, flaky test or hack signals that nobody cares, lowering everyone's standards. Fix small issues quickly to keep the norm high.

first_principles.problem: A codebase with 300 lint warnings gets the 301st without a second thought; one TODO hack becomes the template for the next.
truths: Norms are set by what people see.
derivation: Make **standards visible** and enforced by tools.

analogy.title: One broken window
analogy.story: A building with one unrepaired broken window soon has many, because it signals no one is watching.
analogy.breaks: The original theory is debated in criminology, but the norm-setting effect in codebases is easy to observe.

example.title: Lint warnings creeping up
example.scenario: Warnings grew from 10 to 400 in a year.

steps.label: Mechanism
steps.detail: Making the rule enforced by CI keeps the window fixed.

example.outcome: the codebase stays tidy by default.

check.q: Why does one ignored warning matter?
check.a: It signals that standards aren't enforced, making further neglect more likely.

strategy-1-the-boy-scout-rule.core: "Always leave the code cleaner than you found it." Small improvements in every change (rename, extract, delete dead code, add a test) compound into a healthier codebase without big projects.

first_principles.problem: Big clean-up projects rarely get approved, and code slowly rots between them.
truths: Big refactors are risky and rare.
derivation: In each PR, make **one small improvement** near your change.
Keep it **scoped** so reviews stay easy.
Across a team, this adds up to **hundreds of fixes a year**.

analogy.title: Campsite rule
analogy.story: Leave the campsite cleaner than you found it. If every group picks up a little litter, the site stays clean.
analogy.breaks: Campsite litter is obvious. Code improvements need judgement to keep scope small.

example.title: Fixing a bug in an old module

steps.label: Compounding
steps.detail: Each touch leaves the module slightly better.

check.q: Why do small improvements beat big clean-up projects?
check.a: They're cheap, low-risk and continuous, while big projects are rare and risky.

strategy-2-refactoring-as-hygiene.core: Treat refactoring like brushing your teeth: a small daily habit inside normal work, not a separate project needing approval. Refactor before or as part of feature changes.

first_principles.problem: Teams that ask permission for refactoring 'projects' rarely get it, so debt piles up until a painful rewrite.
truths: Refactoring makes the next change easier.
Delay increases the cost of cleanup.
derivation: **Make the change easy, then make the easy change** (Kent Beck).
Reserve **time each sprint** for larger hygiene.

analogy.title: Brushing teeth daily
analogy.story: Two minutes a day is painless; a once-a-year marathon is too late, the damage is done.
analogy.breaks: Teeth only need brushing. Code also needs occasional bigger structural changes, so reserve some capacity.

example.title: Adding a payment method
example.scenario: The payment code is a 500-line function.

steps.label: Beck's rule
steps.detail: Refactor first so the feature becomes easy.

example.outcome: the feature is quick and the code improves.

check.q: What does 'make the change easy, then make the easy change' mean?
check.a: Refactor first so the new feature fits cleanly, then implement it simply.

strategy-3-automated-entropy-detection.core: Humans get tired; automation doesn't. Linters, static analysis, dependency bots, complexity metrics and architecture tests in CI make decay visible and block it from merging.

first_principles.problem: Code reviews miss subtle decay under deadline pressure, so standards erode PR by PR.

analogy.title: Smoke detectors
analogy.story: You don't rely on people noticing smoke; detectors watch 24/7 and sound the alarm early.
analogy.breaks: Smoke detectors rarely false-alarm. Noisy checks get ignored, so keep them high-signal.

example.title: A complexity ratchet

steps.label: Ratchet
steps.detail: The number can only go down, so improvements stick.

code.text:
# .github/workflows/quality.yml (excerpt)
- run: ruff check .
- run: radon cc src -a --min C   # fail on high complexity

example.outcome: decay is caught automatically before it lands.

check.a: A CI rule that lets a metric improve but never get worse.
